summary: Hosts on IPv6-only networks that use IPv4-IPv6 translation need to know the NAT64 prefix used to build synthesized addresses. This informational document gives guidelines for discovering that prefix, recommending that it be obtained from the Router Advertisement option described in RFC 8781.

eli5.summary: If you want to reach someone in another country, you need the right dialing code. This tells devices the best way to learn the code their network uses.

questions: how to discover the nat64 prefix
why prefer router advertisements for nat64 prefix
subtitle: Why IPv6-only hosts should learn the NAT64 prefix from Router Advertisements instead of asking DNS.

tldr.problem: Hosts on IPv6-only networks that use IPv4-IPv6 translation need to know the NAT64 prefix (PREF64), and the older DNS64-based way of finding it has several weaknesses.
tldr.mechanism: Endpoints SHOULD take PREF64 from the Router Advertisement option defined in RFC 8781, and operators deploying NAT64 SHOULD send it. The DNS64-based method of RFC 7050 stays only as a fallback.
tldr.outcome: The RA option removes the dependence on network-provided resolvers, shortens start-up, lets operators change the prefix immediately and avoids spoofed DNS answers.

today: RFC 9872 is an Informational document published in September 2025, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It points to RFC 8781 as the preferred way to deliver the NAT64 prefix.

sections.title: Why Endpoints Need the NAT64 Prefix
sections.content:
A NAT64 translator maps IPv4 addresses into IPv6 address space using a prefix, called PREF64 (written Pref64::/n). On a network that provides NAT64, it helps endpoints to know that prefix. With it they can run the customer-side translator (CLAT) of 464XLAT (RFC 6877), turn IPv4 literals into IPv6 literals, perform local DNS64 (RFC 6147) functions, and support applications that rely on IPv4 address referral.

Discovery needs to be dynamic so that the configuration stays current, especially for unmanaged endpoints and endpoints that move between networks. RFC 7050 gave the first, DNS64-based method. RFC 8781 later defined a Neighbor Discovery option for Router Advertisements (RAs) that carries PREF64 to hosts, with the advantage that it shares fate with the other network configuration a host receives.
sections.eli5: A translator needs a special address prefix to turn old-style addresses into new-style ones. Devices on the network need to know which prefix is in use, and this RFC says how they should find out.

sections.title: What Endpoints Should Do
sections.content:
Endpoints SHOULD try to get PREF64 from RAs as described in RFC 8781, rather than using the method in RFC 7050. If no PREF64 information appears in the RAs, an endpoint MAY fall back to the RFC 7050 mechanism.

The document also asks implementations to strive for consistent PREF64 acquisition methods. The DNS64-based mechanism should be used only when RA-based delivery is unavailable, or as a fallback for legacy systems that cannot process the PREF64 RA option.
sections.eli5: First listen to what the router says. Only if the router says nothing should a device try the older way of asking around.

sections.title: What Operators Should Do
sections.content:
Network operators that deploy NAT64 SHOULD provide PREF64 information in Router Advertisements per RFC 8781.

Mobile networks. Support for the option is widely built into modern mobile operating systems, but equipment in mobile networks often cannot put the PREF64 option into RAs. The document therefore says its recommendations are not presently applicable to mobile network operators, and encourages them to adopt the option when infrastructure or software upgrades make it practical.

Migration. Moving from the RFC 7050 heuristic to the RA option may need a period where both coexist, depending on how many endpoints run outdated operating systems. Operators are advised to weigh this before removing the old method. Adding RA support is always safe, because endpoints that follow the RFC requirements prefer it over the old method. Leaving DNS64-based discovery also removes DNSSEC and DNS64 incompatibility concerns.
sections.eli5: Network owners should have their routers announce the prefix. Phone networks may not be able to yet, and everyone moving over should keep the old way working until the last old device is gone.

sections.title: Problems with the DNS64-Based Method
sections.content:
The document lists issues with RFC 7050 that the RA option addresses:

  • Resolver dependency. The endpoint must use the network's DNS64 resolvers, or its resolver must treat ipv4only.arpa. as a special name (RFC 8880). Very few implementations do. VPN software that forces DNS through enterprise servers, which typically lack DNS64, can break discovery, especially with split tunneling.
  • Start-up delay. A host with only a DNS-based method needs at least one extra round-trip after the stack is configured. Until then, IPv4-only applications and IPv4-only destinations are impaired.
  • Slow updates. The node caches replies and repeats discovery ten seconds before the TTL of the synthetic AAAA record expires. An operator cannot force rediscovery without disconnecting the node, and may not control the TTL of an external DNS64 server.
  • Multihoming. A node cannot reliably map a prefix learned from DNS to a particular upstream, so it may pick the wrong source address or uplink. RA-delivered prefixes can be tracked per router.

If the network's DNS64 and the endpoint's resolver both use the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96, the endpoint ends up with a valid prefix. After a move to another network, though, it cannot tell whether the new one lacks NAT64 or uses a network-specific prefix.
sections.eli5: Asking a third party for the answer can go wrong in many ways: the person you ask might not know, might answer slowly, or might give an old answer. Hearing it straight from the router avoids all that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNS-based discovery is prone to DNS spoofing attacks, as RFC 7050 itself notes. It also requires a "secure channel" to the DNS64 server. The document argues this is redundant when RAs can already be defended, for example with RA-Guard (RFC 6105), and that making nodes implement two defenses creates unnecessary risk. Of the two example channels in RFC 7050, an IPsec VPN is not supported as a practice by any common operating system DNS client, and link-layer encryption leaves the DNS traffic readable by any node along the path.

Getting PREF64 from RAs therefore mitigates all attack vectors that rely on a spoofed or rogue DNS response. Security considerations for the option itself are in Section 7 of RFC 8781. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Someone could trick a device by faking the answer it gets from the phone book. Getting the answer from the router, which can be protected, is safer.
